title: How do you manage configuration and secrets (ConfigMap vs Secret), and why don't pods pick up a changed ConfigMap/Secret automatically (need a rollout/restart or a reloader)?
shortTitle: ConfigMap vs Secret, and Why Pods Do Not Auto-Reload Config Changes
topicTitle: How do you manage configuration and secrets

s1_definition.profdef: A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs, while a Secret stores sensitive data such as passwords and tokens, base64-encoded and ideally encrypted at rest with restricted RBAC. Both can be consumed by a Pod as environment variables or as mounted files. Environment-variable injection is read once at container start, so an env-based value never changes without a Pod restart. A volume-mounted ConfigMap or Secret is updated on disk by the kubelet after a delay, but the running process has usually already cached the value, so most applications still need a rollout or a reloader to actually apply a change.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a ConfigMap is the branch's public notice board — the daily interest rate, the office hours, the API timeout — anyone can read it. A Secret is the vault combination and the signing stamp, kept locked, logged, and shown only to authorized staff. The reason a teller does not notice when you quietly change the notice board is that the teller memorized the rate when they clocked in this morning; to use the new rate they must clock out and clock back in. That clock-out-clock-in is the Pod restart.
s1_definition.oneliner: ConfigMap holds open settings, Secret holds sensitive values, and neither reliably takes effect without a Pod restart or a reloader because env vars are read once and file caches are stale.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs, while a Secret stores sensitive data such as passwords and tokens, base64-encoded and ideally encrypted at rest with restricted RBAC. Both can be consumed by a Pod as environment variables or as mounted files. Environment-variable injection is read once at container start, so an env-based value never changes without a Pod restart. A volume-mounted ConfigMap or Secret is updated on disk by the kubelet after a delay, but the running process has usually already cached the value, so most applications still need a rollout or a reloader to actually apply a change.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a ConfigMap is the branch's public notice board — the daily interest rate, the office hours, the API timeout — anyone can read it. A Secret is the vault combination and the signing stamp, kept locked, logged, and shown only to authorized staff. The reason a teller does not notice when you quietly change the notice board is that the teller memorized the rate when they clocked in this morning; to use the new rate they must clock out and clock back in. That clock-out-clock-in is the Pod restart.

**One line to remember:** ConfigMap holds open settings, Secret holds sensitive values, and neither reliably takes effect without a Pod restart or a reloader because env vars are read once and file caches are stale.

sections.s2_technical:
A ConfigMap is for data that is not secret: feature flags, log levels, timeouts, upstream URLs, and the application configuration file itself. A Secret is for data that must be protected: database passwords, API keys, TLS private keys, JWT signing keys. The two look similar in YAML, but a Secret's values are base64-encoded (encoding is not encryption), should be encrypted at rest by enabling etcd encryption or an external provider, and should be tightly locked down with RBAC so only the owning service account can read them. In a bank I never put a database password in a ConfigMap.

There are two ways to consume either object. As environment variables, using `envFrom` or `valueFrom`, the values are copied into the process environment at container startup. As a volume mount, the ConfigMap or Secret appears as files in a directory. The consumption mode is exactly what determines reload behaviour.

Environment variables are a point-in-time snapshot. The container's environment is fixed when the process starts, so if you edit the ConfigMap afterward, the running container keeps the old value forever. The only way to pick up the new value is to restart the Pod. This is the most common surprise for newcomers.

Volume-mounted values are different but still tricky. The kubelet periodically syncs the mounted files, so after a delay (up to about a minute, and never for a `subPath` mount, which does not update at all) the file on disk reflects the new ConfigMap. However, most applications read a config file once at startup into memory and never re-read it, so even though the file changed, the process is still using the cached value. Unless the application explicitly watches the file and hot-reloads, nothing changes behaviourally.

So how do you actually apply a change? The explicit, auditable way is to trigger a rollout: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/payment-service`, which recreates the Pods so they read the new config at startup. A cleaner pattern is to make config immutable and versioned: create a new ConfigMap name per release, for example `payment-config-v7`, reference it in the Pod template, and let the normal rolling update apply it, which also means a Deployment rollback automatically points back at the old config. For automatic reloads, tools like Reloader or Stakater watch ConfigMaps and Secrets and trigger a rollout when they change, and some frameworks like Spring Cloud Kubernetes can watch and refresh beans. The senior point is that implicit auto-reload of a live Secret in a payment service is usually undesirable anyway: you want config changes to go through a controlled, logged rollout, not silently mutate a running process handling money.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Payment Service reads a daily transfer fee from configuration and a database password from a secret. Two real problems drove this scenario.

Problem 1 — an operator edited the ConfigMap to raise the transfer fee, then was puzzled that transfers kept charging the old fee for an hour. The service had read the fee as an environment variable at startup, so it never saw the change. This is exactly why env-injected config needs a restart.

Problem 2 — we stored the database password as a mounted Secret. When security rotated the password, the running Pods kept using the old one from their cached in-memory copy and started failing authentication until we restarted them. This is exactly why even mounted Secrets need a rollout or a reloader.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `PaymentService` that caches a fee from an env-style `ConfigSource` at construction (snapshot behaviour) and reads a password from a `SecretSource`. A `ConfigMapStore` and `SecretStore` can be mutated at runtime, and a `Reloader` shows the difference between a silent file change (no effect) and a triggered restart (new value applied). We process a transfer for Rajesh and Priya before and after a config change to prove the snapshot behaviour.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the config reload simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/config/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.config.ConfigReloadDemo

# Real cluster: apply a config change and actually make it take effect
kubectl edit configmap payment-config-v7              # edit transfer.fee
kubectl rollout restart deployment/payment-service    # Pods re-read config
# Or install Reloader so a ConfigMap/Secret change auto-triggers the rollout
helm install reloader stakater/reloader
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Payment Service starts with a fee of 20, then an operator raises it to 35.

Step 1 — The ConfigMap holds `transfer.fee=20` and the Secret holds the database password. The PaymentService constructor reads the fee once into an immutable field and caches the password. This mirrors env-variable injection, which is a startup snapshot.

Step 2 — Rajesh transfers fifty thousand rupees to Priya. The service debits fifty thousand plus the cached fee of 20, so twenty rupees of fee is applied.

Step 3 — The operator edits the ConfigMap to `transfer.fee=35`. The store logs that the change touched the ConfigMap but is disk-only. The running service's field is unchanged.

Step 4 — Rajesh transfers again. The service still uses the cached fee of 20, not 35. The log raises a warning that the change was not applied because the env-style value was frozen at startup. This is the exact surprise that confuses operators.

Step 5 — A rollout restart is triggered. The Reloader constructs a fresh PaymentService, which re-reads the ConfigMap and now caches a fee of 35. The next transfer applies the new fee of 35. The change only took effect through a restart.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 00:54:50.104 [INFO] ConfigMap edited: transfer.fee=35 (disk only!)
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ConfigMap(fee=20) + Secret(db.password)
    │ consumed as ENV at container START (snapshot)
    ▼
  PaymentService (fee cached = 20)
    │ transfer → fee 20 applied ✓
    │
  Operator edits ConfigMap → fee=35
    │ (env value does NOT change; mounted file would lag + be cached)
    ▼
  PaymentService still fee=20  ✗ (no effect)
    │
  kubectl rollout restart  /  Reloader auto-trigger
    ▼
  NEW Pod re-reads ConfigMap → fee cached = 35 ✓
    │ transfer → fee 35 applied ✓
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I manage configuration with ConfigMaps and sensitive data with Secrets, and I keep the line between them strict. A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive settings like log levels, timeouts, feature flags, and upstream URLs. A Secret holds anything that must be protected, such as database passwords, API keys, and TLS private keys. A Secret's values are only base64-encoded, which is encoding and not encryption, so in a bank I also enable encryption at rest for etcd or use an external provider like Vault, and I lock the Secret down with tight RBAC so only the owning service account can read it. I never put a credential in a ConfigMap.

Both can be consumed as environment variables or as mounted files, and that choice is exactly what determines reload behaviour. Environment variables are a startup snapshot: the container's environment is fixed when the process starts, so editing the ConfigMap afterward has no effect on a running Pod and the only way to apply it is a restart. Volume-mounted values do get refreshed on disk by the kubelet after a delay, except for subPath mounts which never update, but the application has almost always already read the file once into memory, so unless it actively watches and hot-reloads, the running process keeps using the stale value.

That is precisely why Pods do not silently pick up config and secret changes, and in a payment system I actually consider that a feature rather than a bug. I want configuration changes to go through a controlled, auditable rollout, not to silently mutate a process that is moving customers' money. So I apply changes with a rollout restart, or I make configuration immutable and versioned by creating a new ConfigMap name per release and referencing it from the Pod template, which also means a rollback automatically reverts to the matching old config. For cases that genuinely need automation, I install a reloader that watches ConfigMaps and Secrets and triggers the rollout for me.

In my project at the National Bank of India this came up twice. An operator raised the transfer fee in a ConfigMap and was baffled that transfers kept charging the old fee, because the service had read it as an environment variable at startup. And when security rotated the database password in a mounted Secret, the running Pods kept using the cached old credential and failed authentication until we restarted them. Both incidents reinforced the same discipline: treat config and secret changes as deployments, apply them through a rollout or a reloader, and never assume a live edit reaches a running Pod on its own.
